newsitem.title: INDIA: Cheaper cotton prices boost Indian textiles.
newsitem.headline: Cheaper cotton prices boost Indian textiles.

text.p: India's ailing textile mills are heading for better times, boosted by lower costs after a record cotton crop, more high-value products and rising exports, industry officials and analysts said on Sunday.
"We should see overall growth (in output) of 10 percent this year (1996/97, April-March)," said Renuka Ramnath, group manager for corporate finance at ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd.
The textile sector, which accounts for one-fifth of India's industrial production and more than a third of its exports, usually has a 3.0-4.0 percent annual increase in growth, she said.
Analysts said the higher growth this year was due to cheaper cotton prices since domestic sales continue to be sluggish.
"Cotton prices have come down by 15-20 percent this year," B.M. Shah, vice president, corporate finance, at Arvind Mills told Reuters. "From its peak levels last year, it is down 40 percent."

This has helped push up gross margins to 20 percent for Arvind Mills, the world's fifth largest denim maker, after it dipped to 11 percent in 1995/96, managing director Sanjay Lalbhai told a news conference on Saturday.
Textile exports during April-June 1996 were $2.25 billion against $2.00 billion in the year-ago period, according to estmates by India's Textile Export Promotion Council.
"The outlook is good for cotton textiles," said Rajiv Saxena, head of research at Lazard Creditcapital Research Ltd.
"The bumper (cotton) crop means the industry is assured of a comfortable carry- over stock position. It is the best hedge against any upsurge in the following year," he said.
Latest estimates peg 1995/96 (September-August) cotton production at 12.3 million 480-lb bales, or 15.7 million 170-kg (375-lb) bales. The earlier forecast was 11.9 million 480-bales.
India, the world's biggest cotton grower, had 8.6 million hectares (21.4 million acres) under cultivation in 1995/96 (September-August), up from 7.8 million hectares (19.3 million acres) in 1994/95.
But the yield at 310 kg per hectare was sharply lower than the global average of 560 kg, said Suresh Kotak, president of the East India Cotton Association.

The synthetic segment (man-made fibres) of the textile industry has been hit by falling world prices and lower import duties. But blended fabrics, popular with the upper end of the market, are holding their own, analysts said.
In its 1996/97 federal budget, India cut import duties to 10 percent for textile machinery imports while the duty for imports by other industries was pegged at 25 percent.

The textile industry is slowly modernising, adding new technology and linking up with foreign firms, and could benefit from the tearing down of tariffs and quotas that now stunt its growth, analysts said.
